explain.say: In 1954 two Comet jet airliners broke up in flight. The cause was fatigue: cracks that grew, cycle by cycle, from the corners of windows and cut-outs in the cabin. Bend a paperclip back and forth and it snaps, though one bend would never break it. Look at how a fatigue failure grows.

draw.text: Fatigue: failure under repeated stress well below the static strength

explain.say: Cracks start where stress is concentrated, at a hole, a sharp corner or a scratch. Each cycle opens the crack a tiny bit more, leaving beach marks on the broken face. Finally the remaining metal is too small and it snaps suddenly. Which do you think matters more: the peak load or the number of cycles?

explain.say: Both, and the S–N curve links them. S is the stress amplitude, N is the cycles to failure, plotted on a log scale. See the falling line? For a steel of 600 megapascals tensile strength, about 540 megapascals gives a thousand cycles. At 400 megapascals it lasts roughly 34,000.

explain.say: Now the magic. Steel flattens out near 10 to the 6 cycles, at about half its tensile strength: 300 megapascals here. Below this endurance limit, a polished test bar lasts essentially forever. See the flat part? Aluminium, the other curve, keeps falling, with no true limit. So what must aircraft makers do?

explain.say: Design aluminium parts for a set number of cycles, and inspect and replace them! Superb. Exam tip: real parts are weaker than test bars, so the endurance limit is reduced by factors for surface finish, size and reliability. Smooth corners and polished surfaces help a lot.

faq.a: Failure caused by many cycles of stress well below the static strength. A crack starts at a stress raiser and grows a little each cycle until the part breaks suddenly.

faq.q: How do I read an S-N curve?
faq.a: Find the stress amplitude on the vertical axis, move across to the curve, and read down to the number of cycles to failure, usually on a log scale.

faq.q: Does aluminium have an endurance limit?
faq.a: No. Aluminium alloys keep losing strength with more cycles, so designers quote a fatigue strength at a set number of cycles, such as 500 million.
For steels, the stress amplitude below which a polished test bar can survive an essentially unlimited number of cycles. It is roughly half the tensile strength for many steels.
At stress raisers: holes, sharp corners, keyways, threads, weld toes and surface scratches, where the local stress is much higher than average.

facts: The de Havilland Comet accidents of 1954 were traced to fatigue cracking of the pressurised cabin.
For many steels the endurance limit of a polished test bar is about half the ultimate tensile strength.

quiz.say: A steel has an ultimate tensile strength of 800 megapascals. Roughly what is the endurance limit of a polished test bar?
quiz.show: Steel with Sut = 800 MPa. Approximate endurance limit (polished bar)?
quiz.why: For steels below about 1400 MPa, Se′ ≈ 0.5 × Sut = 400 MPa.

wrong.1: Fatigue strength is well below the static tensile strength.
wrong.2: That is far too low for a polished steel bar.
